newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: SECURITY COUNCIL PANEL RECEIVES IRAQI OIL PRICES.
newsitem.headline: SECURITY COUNCIL PANEL RECEIVES IRAQI OIL PRICES.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council's sanctions committee on Wednesday received Iraq's oil pricing formula, which had been approved by U.N. experts or overseers, U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said.
The committee now has 48 hours -- until 1100 EDT/1500 GMT Friday -- to raise any objections, he said. Otherwise the formula is accepted and Iraq can resume oil sales.

"The U.N. overseers have submitted to the committee the new oil pricing formula which they received from Iraq and which will govern the sale of Iraqi oil," he said. "The committee has 48 hours to examine the formula."

The oil pricing formula moves Iraq closer to resuming sales under a U.N. plan that allows Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil every three months to buy food, medicine and other goods for its people to ease the effects of sanctions.

Iraq had delayed in submitting the pricing formula until U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan approved Baghdad's program to distribute the humanitarian goods. He did so on Monday and Iraq now has to sell $1 billion in oil by September 5.
The oil-for-food plan first went into effect last December and was renewed for another six months on June 8, with oil sales divided into two 90-day or three month periods.
The program is an exception to U.N. sanctions imposed on Iraq after its troops invaded Kuwait seven years ago.
The United Nations did not reveal the prices.

But industry and diplomatic sources said Tuesday that Iraq reduced prices for Basrah Light and Kirkuk crude oil after initial objections from the U.N. overseers who conferred by telephone with officials from the Iraq State Oil and Marketing Organization (SOMO) before the plan was submitted in writing.

Under the new rates, Basrah Light to the United States. is now priced at $4.50 under West Texas Intermediate for August on an FOB basis. Kirkuk to Europe is at Dated Brent -$1.90, and at WTI -$3.50 for the United States.
Asian customers received a price for Basrah Light at an average of Oman/Dubai -55 cents, the sources said, also on an FOB basis for August.

SOMO had first proposed a price of $4.40 per barrel under regional benchmark WTI for U.S. buyers of its Basrah Light, according to traders with oil companies that had contracts with Iraq earlier in the year.

That was up from a discount of $4.60 in May, when crude was last lifted from Mina al Bakr in the Middle East Gulf, and in line with the 20 cents rise in Saudi Arabian Light crude, which SOMO had been tracking in the first round.
Oil traders said that Iraq's original pricing formula was too high, given a rise in freight costs in the past two months and the difficulty in marketing a large amount of Iraqi crude.
